subject: English Language
source: AQA GCSE English Language 8700 specification and syllabus data file (content/syllabus/ks4/english-language.json). Supplements and does not duplicate the existing y11.json (which covers P2 Q1-Q5 well); these lessons add modelling lessons around a new original source pair (Source A modern column, Source B 1871-style letter, both written for TGA) and cover the Spoken Language endorsement (SL), which existing lessons do not cover.

lessons.unit: P2-A-Q1: Paper 2 Section A: Question 1, true statements
lessons.title: Question 1: choosing the four true statements
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I judge a statement is true when it sounds almost right?
objectives: Read a Paper 2 Question 1 and find evidence for each statement in the named lines
Tell the difference between true, false and 'sounds true' statements
Complete the question quickly and accurately
successCriteria: All: select statements supported by the text
Most: reject statements with one small error
Some: justify each choice by line number in under four minutes
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: reading survey data (one in five, nearly half)
lessons.smsc: Moral: truthfulness and care with evidence (sidq)

keywords.def: a statement fully supported by the text
a statement that looks possible but contains an error

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: what is Paper 2 Question 1 worth and what does it test?
Fractions: what does 'one in five' mean as a fraction and a percentage?
What is the difference between 'a mile' and 'a kilometre'?

teach.heading: Source A

quote.text:
1 Every weekday at 8.15, my street turns into a car park. Engines idle, horns
2 blare, and a small boy is lifted from a 4x4 and set down like a parcel, twenty
3 metres from the school gate. The school is just a mile from our house, but
4 hardly anyone walks it any more. Last year a survey in our town found that
5 only one child in five walked to school; nearly half arrived by car.
6 I understand why. The roads are busier, parents are rushed, and nobody
7 wants to be late for work. Yet I have started walking my daughter, Mina, the
8 whole mile. It takes twenty-five minutes. She complains for the first five,
9 then she begins to notice things: the baker's van, a heron on the canal,
10 the way frost lingers in the shade. By the gate she is calmer and
11 chatting. I am convinced that those twenty-five minutes teach her more
12 than any worksheet.
quote.source: Source A: original 21st-century newspaper column written for TGA

teach.note: Read aloud. Pupils number the lines. All sources in this unit are original and written for TGA. Cultural context: the school run is a British phrase for the morning trip to school; a 4x4 is a large car; 'frost' is ice crystals on cold mornings. Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart.

teach.heading: The Question 1 routine
cycle: Underline the key word or number in each statement
Find the matching line in the stated lines
Tick only if every part is supported
Stop at four; check numbers and quantifiers
teach.note: Say: four marks, four statements; if more than four are chosen, only the first four are marked, so do not over-choose. Teach pupils to underline the key detail in each statement and match it to a line. Ask which words hide errors: 'all', 'never', 'always', 'only', numbers.

teach.heading: Worked model

model.problem: Read lines 1 to 8. Choose four statements that are true. A: The school is two miles away. B: A boy is lifted from a large car. C: Nearly half of children arrive by car. D: Hardly anyone walks to school. E: Mina walks in five minutes. F: Parents are rushed.
steps: A: line 3 says 'just a mile', so A is false.
B: lines 1-2 say a small boy is lifted from a 4x4, so B is true.
C: line 5 says nearly half arrived by car, so C is true.
D: line 4 says 'hardly anyone walks', so D is true; E: line 8 says twenty-five minutes, so E is false; F: line 6 says 'parents are rushed', so F is true.
model.answer: True: B, C, D and F. (A and E are false.)

teach.note: Walk through each statement. Point out trap A has a changed number and C has a reversed fact. Link the idea of explicit to AO1: the evidence is in the text.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which statement is true according to lines 4 to 8?
options: One child in four walks to school.
Mina walks to school without complaining.
The walk takes twenty-five minutes.
check.why: C matches line 8. A changes the number in line 5; B ignores 'She complains for the first five'.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is C. A changes 'one in five' to 'one in four'; B contradicts line 8.

teach.heading: Common error

misconception.wrong: 'Hardly anyone walks' is the same as 'nobody walks', so it is false.
misconception.right: 'Hardly anyone' means very few, which matches line 4; read each statement against the exact words.

teach.note: Ask pupils to read the statement twice. Say that one wrong word makes the whole statement false. Idiom: 'the devil is in the detail'.

practice: Using lines 6 to 12, write two true statements and two false statements for a partner.
Mark a partner's statements and write the line number for each answer.
Decide: 'Mina notices a heron on the canal.' True or false? Give the line.
independent: Core: Complete an original Question 1: lines 6 to 12, eight statements, choose four true.
Extend: Write your own eight statements for lines 1 to 5 with a tick list.
Stretch: Rewrite three false statements as true ones and explain the changes.
exit: How many statements should you choose?
Why must you check numbers and 'only' or 'all'?
Big question: how do I decide a statement is true?
lessons.homework: Write eight statements (four true, four false) for a news report you find and swap with a family member.
lessons.send: SEND: enlarge the text, add line numbers and allow a ruler to track lines; give a tick-box table with the line number column. EAL/international: pre-teach 'idle', 'blare', 'lingers', 'canal'; idiom 'the school run' and 'the devil is in the detail'; stems: 'Line 4 says that ...', 'This is false because ...'. Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart. Stretch: write a statement that is true but implicit, not explicit.

lessons.unit: P2-A-Q2: Paper 2 Section A: Question 2, summary
lessons.title: Question 2: a model summary of differences across two sources
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I merge two texts into one clear answer without listing quotations?
objectives: Select the differences that answer the specific focus of the question
Infer meaning rather than copy details
Write in continuous prose using comparative language
successCriteria: All: write two differences with evidence
Most: use comparative connectives and infer meaning
Some: synthesise both sources in a single, concise paragraph
lessons.crossCurricular: History: the 1870 Education Act and daily life
lessons.smsc: Social: understanding how childhood has changed

keywords.def: what the question asks you to concentrate on

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: how many marks is Paper 2 Question 2 and what is its AO?
Write a sentence using 'whereas' to contrast a cat and a dog.
Name two differences between a letter and a newspaper column.

teach.heading: Both sources

quote.text:
1 Thornbury, 14th October 1871
2 My dear Sister,
3 You ask how the children fare at the new school, and I am glad to say they thrive,
4 though I confess the road to it is no light matter. Every morning, whatever the weather,
5 Thomas and little Ellen must walk the full three miles by the old turnpike, with their
6 dinner in a tin and their boots, I fear, scarcely sound. In November the lane is a
7 river of mud, and last week Ellen arrived with her stockings quite sodden, and was
8 scolded by the mistress for the state of her pinafore. Yet I would not keep them at home.
9 Education is the only fortune a poor man's child may hope to inherit, and I shall not
10 see it wasted for want of a little weariness in the legs. Thomas says the walk is the best
11 part of the day, for he and the Pritchard boys race the carrier's cart, and he knows where
12 every bird builds its nest.
13 Pray give my love to Papa, and believe me, your affectionate sister, Eliza
quote.source: Source B: original letter in the style of 1871, written for TGA (pastiche, not a real historical document)

teach.note: Reprint Source A (lines 1-12) and Source B (lines 1-13) for pupils. Say this lesson uses both. Source B has unfamiliar details; 'turnpike' (toll road), 'pinafore' (child's overall), 'mistress' (teacher), 'sodden' (soaking wet). Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart.

teach.heading: The focus and the plan
teach.note: Give the question and ask pupils to colour-code differences in two colours. Note that the question asks only for differences in how children travel to school, so facts about the parents' feelings are not needed. Pupils should refer to both sources in every sentence, not write two paragraphs about two texts.

teach.heading: Worked model: an eight-mark summary

model.problem: Write a summary of the differences between the way children travel to school in Source A and Source B. (8 marks)
steps: State the focus: the way children get to school.
Pair the evidence: one mile versus three miles; car versus foot.
Infer: Source A implies walking is now a choice; Source B implies it is a necessity.
Use comparative connectives: whereas, in contrast, while.
Close with a synthesised point.
model.answer: In Source A most children are driven the short mile to school, whereas the children in Source B have no choice but to walk three miles in all weathers. The modern parent chooses to walk, which suggests walking is now a deliberate habit, while in 1871 it is an unavoidable hardship, shown by the 'river of mud' and unsound boots. In contrast to the calm, observant Mina, Thomas turns the journey into a race with the carrier's cart. The sources therefore show a shift from necessity to choice.

teach.note: Model aloud; underline the comparative words and the inferences (in italics). Note that the paragraph never copies more than two words in a row. Time guide: about ten minutes.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is the best opening sentence?
options: 'Source A says the street is a car park and Source B says it is a river of mud.'
'In Source A most children are driven a short distance, whereas in Source B they must walk three miles.'
'Both parents love their children.'
check.why: B answers the focus and compares in one sentence. A lists quotations; C is off focus.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is B. A is a list of quotations; C is about attitudes, not the focus.

teach.heading: Inference ladder
bullets: Detail: boots, I fear, scarcely sound.
Inference: the family cannot afford good boots.
Link: in Source A, parents choose cars.
Difference: poverty then, convenience now.
teach.note: Show how a detail becomes inference: 'boots scarcely sound' leads to 'the family are poor and cannot afford proper boots'.

practice: Write a sentence of difference about time using 'whereas'.
Infer one thing from 'dinner in a tin' and compare with Source A.
Colour-code a partner's sentence for evidence and inference.
independent: Core: Write a six-sentence summary of the differences in travel to school.
Extend: Write a summary of differences in the conditions the children face, with inference.
Stretch: Write a 150-word summary that also synthesises the changes over time.
exit: Name two comparative connectives.
Why is a list of quotations not a summary?
Big question: how do I merge two texts into one answer?
lessons.homework: Write a 100-word summary of the differences between a school day now and 100 years ago, using whichever sources you can find (a family member, a library book).
lessons.send: SEND: give a comparison table and sentence starters; limit to four sentences. EAL/international: pre-teach 'turnpike', 'pinafore', 'mistress', 'sodden', 'unavoidable'; idiom 'to come down to' = to depend; stems: 'In Source A ..., whereas in Source B ...', 'This suggests that ...'. Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart. Stretch: include a counter-point where the sources are similar.

lessons.unit: P2-A-Q3: Paper 2 Section A: Question 3, language
lessons.title: Question 3: language in a 19th-century letter
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a writer's choice of words reveal her feelings and persuade us?
objectives: Decode 19th-century vocabulary and sentence structures
Analyse tone, understatement and metaphor for effect
Write a Level 4 paragraph on a non-fiction source
successCriteria: All: quote and explain a word's effect
Most: analyse tone and method with terminology
Some: link language to the writer's purpose and attitude in a sustained paragraph
lessons.smsc: Moral: sacrifice and aspiration (a parent's hope for children)

keywords.def: the attitude or mood of the writing
saying less than the truth to emphasise it
understatement using a negative, such as 'no light matter'

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name two differences between Source A and Source B (last lesson).
Define 'tone' using two adjectives.
What is the effect of a metaphor?

teach.heading: Decode the letter

quote.text:
1 Thornbury, 14th October 1871
2 My dear Sister,
3 You ask how the children fare at the new school, and I am glad to say they thrive,
4 though I confess the road to it is no light matter. Every morning, whatever the weather,
5 Thomas and little Ellen must walk the full three miles by the old turnpike, with their
6 dinner in a tin and their boots, I fear, scarcely sound. In November the lane is a
7 river of mud, and last week Ellen arrived with her stockings quite sodden, and was
8 scolded by the mistress for the state of her pinafore. Yet I would not keep them at home.
9 Education is the only fortune a poor man's child may hope to inherit, and I shall not
10 see it wasted for want of a little weariness in the legs. Thomas says the walk is the best
11 part of the day, for he and the Pritchard boys race the carrier's cart, and he knows where
12 every bird builds its nest.
13 Pray give my love to Papa, and believe me, your affectionate sister, Eliza
quote.source: Source B: original letter in the style of 1871, written for TGA (pastiche, not a real historical document)

teach.note: Reprint Source B for pupils. Read it with a warm, formal voice. Ask: what is the mother's attitude to the long walk, and how can you tell from the first paragraph? Use idiom: 'no light matter' = a serious thing. Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart.

teach.heading: Method: tone, technique, effect
cycle: Explain the effect on the reader
Link to the writer's purpose and attitude
teach.note: Remind pupils that Question 3 (12 marks) is on one source only and the same Q-M-E-Z routine applies. In Paper 2 attitude and purpose matter; so every comment links to the writer's point of view. Ask pupils to find three words where the tone shifts from worry to resolve.

teach.heading: Worked model: a Level 4 paragraph

model.problem: How does the writer use language to show her attitude to the children's walk to school? (12 marks)
steps: Tone: the formal 'I confess' creates a dutiful, honest tone.
Litotes: 'no light matter' understates the difficulty, so the hardship feels gently stated, not exaggerated.
Metaphor: 'a river of mud' vividly shows the dangers of the lane.
Metaphor: 'the only fortune a poor man's child may hope to inherit' turns education into wealth.
Zoom: 'weariness' is small and manageable, so she dismisses the hardship.
model.answer: The writer adopts a formal, dutiful tone from the outset: 'I confess' suggests honest admission, as though she is reluctant to burden her sister with complaints. The litotes 'no light matter' understates the difficulty, so the reader senses a hardship stoically accepted. The metaphor 'a river of mud' is vivid and slightly comic, but it also emphasises how dangerous the lane is for a small child. Yet she refuses to keep the children at home, calling education 'the only fortune a poor man's child may hope to inherit'. The metaphor of wealth shows that, for this family, learning is the only route to security, so the mother's pride outweighs her worry. The understated 'a little weariness in the legs' dismisses the hardship, which implies a stern determination that the reader admires.

teach.note: Read twice and ask for the zoomed words ('confess', 'inherit'). Point out that this paragraph deals with two features and the shift, and about 150 words is realistic. Mention that 'no light matter' is litotes (understatement using a negative).

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: What is the effect of 'a little weariness in the legs'?
options: It understates the hardship, showing the mother's determination.
It states that the children are strong.
It is an example of onomatopoeia.
check.why: A explains the understatement and its effect on tone. B is not supported; C is incorrect (no sound).

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is A. B ignores the effect; C names a feature not in the text.

teach.heading: Terminology bank
bullets: tone: dutiful, stoical, affectionate, firm
method: litotes, metaphor, hyperbole, direct address
effect: reassures, persuades, evokes sympathy
link: purpose and attitude
teach.note: Stress that terminology supports analysis; it does not replace it. Offer EAL pupils the sentence frames.

practice: Analyse 'whatever the weather' in one Q-M-E-Z sentence.
What is the effect of 'dinner in a tin'?
Identify one formal word and explain why it fits the period.
independent: Core: Write a four-sentence paragraph on the metaphor 'a river of mud'.
Extend: Write a full paragraph (150 words) on tone and understatement.
Stretch: Write a two-paragraph answer analysing how the tone changes from worry to resolve.
exit: Name two methods in Source B.
Why is 'no light matter' called understatement?
Big question: how does a writer's language reveal her feelings?
lessons.homework: Write a 100-word letter in the style of Source B about a modern problem and list three formal features you used.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a three-column analysis grid (quote, method, effect) and a tone word bank. EAL/international: pre-teach 'dutiful', 'stoical', 'understatement', 'sodden', 'confess'; idiom 'to put a brave face on it' = to hide worry; stems: 'The tone is ... because ...', 'The writer implies ...'. Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart. Stretch: compare the tone with a modern parent's tone in Source A.

lessons.unit: P2-A-Q4: Paper 2 Section A: Question 4, comparison of perspectives
lessons.title: Question 4: writing a comparison of perspectives and methods
lessons.bigQuestion: How do two writers' different worlds shape how they write about the same thing?
objectives: Compare two writers' perspectives with references to both
Compare methods: language and structure
Use comparative connectives to link ideas
successCriteria: All: write about both sources with evidence
Most: compare perspectives and methods using connectives
Some: write a sustained, perceptive comparison tracing perspective, language and structure across both texts
lessons.crossCurricular: History: social change from 1871 to today
lessons.smsc: Social and cultural: empathy across time and place

keywords.def: the position or attitude from which something is seen
a link word showing similarity or difference
the language and structure choices a writer makes

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: write one difference between the two sources about distance.
Name two comparative connectives for similarity and two for difference.
What does AO3 ask for?

teach.heading: The question

quote.text: Compare how the two writers convey their different perspectives and feelings about children walking to school. In your answer, you could: compare their different perspectives and feelings; compare the methods they use to convey their perspectives; support your response with references to both texts. (16 marks)

teach.note: Display the question with both sources available. Ask pupils to underline the key words 'perspectives' and 'methods'. Stress that Q4 is worth 16 marks and uses the whole of both sources. Pupils plan for three minutes then write for about fifteen.

teach.heading: A comparison grid

head: Feature
Source A (column)
Source B (letter)
rows: walking is a hardship worth bearing
report, then resolve, then a joyful detail

teach.note: Fill the grid with pupils. Ask: who is the audience and how does it change the writing? Draw out that Source A is a published column seeking to persuade, Source B a private letter reporting and reassuring. Ask pupils to find a similarity too (both value learning).

teach.heading: Worked model: two comparative paragraphs

model.problem: Compare how the two writers convey their different perspectives and feelings about children walking to school. (16 marks)
steps: Link perspective and method in each paragraph.
Use quotation from both sources every time.
Use connectives: whereas, similarly, in contrast.
Comment on structure as well as language.
Finish with a short overview.
model.answer: Both writers value what children gain on the journey, but they convey this very differently. The modern columnist, who chooses to walk, presents the journey as a gift: the simile of a boy 'set down like a parcel' mocks the car parent, while the calm Mina who notices 'a heron on the canal' shows what is gained. In contrast, the Victorian mother treats the walk as a necessary hardship, conveyed by the metaphor 'a river of mud' and the understatement 'no light matter'. Whereas the column moves from a problem to a personal solution to persuade the public, the letter moves from worry to determination to reassure a sister, ending with the joyful detail of the boys racing the cart. Both therefore see the walk as valuable, but for the columnist it is an escape from modern life, and for Eliza an unavoidable price of education.

teach.note: Read aloud and underline the connectives. Point out every sentence refers to both sources, with quotation and method. Ask where perspective and method are linked.

teach.heading: Hinge question

options: Source A is about cars. Source B is about mud.
Both writers like the walk.
Whereas the columnist chooses to walk, Eliza accepts the walk as unavoidable, shown by 'no light matter'.
check.why: C compares perspectives with a connective and evidence. A is separate; B has no evidence.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is C. A treats the sources separately; B is a similarity without evidence.

teach.heading: Structure comments
bullets: Source A: starts with a problem, ends with a conclusion.
Source B: starts with greeting, ends with warmth.
Both end on a positive image.
Compare: public persuasion versus private reassurance.
teach.note: Remind pupils that Q4 rewards methods, and that structure counts. Ask them to find the shifts.

practice: Write one sentence comparing the tone of the two sources with a connective.
Compare one language method in each source.
Write a sentence comparing the endings.
independent: Core: Write one comparative paragraph on perspective, with quotations from both sources.
Extend: Write two paragraphs: one on perspective, one on methods (language and structure).
Stretch: Write a full 300-word answer with an overview and a perceptive conclusion.
exit: Name three comparative connectives.
Why must every paragraph refer to both sources?
Big question: how do different worlds shape how writers write?
lessons.homework: Write 120 words comparing a modern and an old text of your choice (a family letter and a text message) using three connectives.
lessons.send: SEND: give a pre-filled comparison grid, a connectives bank and a two-paragraph frame. EAL/international: pre-teach 'perspective', 'whereas', 'unavoidable', 'necessity'; idiom 'on the one hand ... on the other hand'; stems: 'Both writers ..., but ...', 'Whereas Source A ..., Source B ...'. Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart. Stretch: add a counter-reading in which the columnist is less sincere.

lessons.unit: P2-A-Q4: Paper 2 Section A: Question 4, comparison of perspectives
lessons.title: Question 4: embedding evidence and weaving methods into comparison
lessons.bigQuestion: How can I make every sentence of a comparison do two jobs at once?
objectives: Embed short quotations within comparative sentences
Combine perspective, method and effect in one sentence
Revise a draft comparison for balance and precision
successCriteria: All: use quotations from both sources in one answer
Most: link a method to a perspective in each sentence
Some: write tightly integrated comparative sentences with perceptive inference
lessons.smsc: Social: listening fairly to different generations

keywords.def: fit a short quotation into your own sentence
combine two ideas in one sentence
a meaning worked out from clues
a short summing-up of the main comparison

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name the three things a Q4 answer compares.
Embed the quotation 'a river of mud' in your own sentence.
Which source is more formal and why?

teach.heading: From a weak to a strong sentence

left.title: Weak (one job)
points: Source A says the street is a car park.
Source B says the road is hard.

right.title: Strong (many jobs)
points: The columnist mocks the car parent with the simile 'like a parcel', whereas Eliza accepts hardship with the understated 'no light matter'.

teach.note: Show the progression. Ask pupils to count the jobs each sentence does (perspective, quotation, method, comparison). Note that weak sentences do one job. Both source texts reprinted in the pack.

teach.heading: Balance check
bullets: Count quotations: A and B equal?
Do both sources appear in each paragraph?
Is there one structure comment each?
Is there one inference about each writer?
teach.note: Say that a lopsided answer (four paragraphs on A, one on B) limits marks. Ask pupils to count references. Stress using short quotations.

teach.heading: Worked model: improving a draft

model.problem: Improve this draft: 'Source A is modern. Source B is old. Source A walks. Source B also walks.'
steps: Replace listing with a comparative sentence.
Add a quotation from each source.
Name a method and its effect for each.
Add an inference about the writer's perspective.
model.answer: Whereas the columnist walks by choice, presenting it as calming through the gentle detail of 'a heron on the canal', Eliza's children walk of necessity, with 'dinner in a tin' implying a family with little money; the contrast shows how walking has changed from hardship to luxury.

teach.note: Look at the revision steps. Ask pupils to read the draft and the revised version aloud and identify what changed. Note that the revision changes 'also' to 'whereas', adds a method and an inference.

teach.heading: Hinge question

options: The columnist uses a simile 'like a parcel' and a list of calm details and a conclusion.
The columnist mocks car drivers with 'like a parcel', whereas Eliza dignifies hardship with 'no light matter'.
Both writers are good at writing.
check.why: B uses evidence from both sources and compares attitude and method. A is about one source; C has no evidence.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is B. A is not balanced; C does not use evidence.

teach.heading: Overview sentence
bullets: Overall, both see value in the journey.
Yet one sees choice, the other necessity.
Methods differ: persuasion versus reassurance.
Write it in 25 words or fewer.
teach.note: End with a single, clear sentence of overview. EAL stem 'Overall, ...'.

practice: Combine two weak sentences into one comparative sentence with quotations.
Write an overview sentence for the two sources.
Count and balance the quotations in a partner's paragraph.
independent: Core: Rewrite a weak comparison paragraph so every sentence has a quotation from each source.
Extend: Write a full paragraph comparing structure, with an inference.
Stretch: Write a timed 250-word answer and self-mark against balance and precision.
exit: What is a quotation that is 'embedded'?
Why must a comparison be balanced?
Big question: how can a sentence do two jobs at once?
lessons.homework: Take your earlier Q4 answer, count quotations from each source, and rewrite one paragraph to make it balanced.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a four-box sentence builder (quotation A, quotation B, connective, effect). EAL/international: pre-teach 'embed', 'integrate', 'balance', 'overview'; idiom 'to kill two birds with one stone'; stems: 'Whereas ..., ...', 'Overall, ...'. Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart. Stretch: compare how each writer addresses the reader (direct address in A, intimate address in B).

lessons.unit: P2-B-Q5: Paper 2 Section B: Question 5, viewpoint writing
lessons.title: Question 5: audience, purpose and form (a modelled article)
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I make my own view sound convincing and suited to the reader?
objectives: Read a Question 5 prompt and identify audience, purpose and form
Plan an article with a clear line of argument
Write a controlled, persuasive opening paragraph
successCriteria: All: state the audience, purpose and form
Most: write an article with a headline, an opening, paragraphs and a conclusion
Some: control register and structure so the article is shaped for its readers
lessons.smsc: Spiritual and social: humility and care for others in how we walk through the world

keywords.def: the people the writing is for
what the writing is meant to do
the type of text, such as article, speech or letter
the title of a newspaper article

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: how many marks are there for content and organisation and how many for technical accuracy?
Name three features of a newspaper article.
What is the difference between audience and purpose?

teach.heading: The task

quote.text: 'Children today should walk or cycle to school instead of being driven.' Write an article for your school magazine in which you explain your point of view on this statement. (40 marks)

teach.note: Display the task. Ask pupils to underline audience (readers of the school magazine), purpose (persuade) and form (article). The task links to the Section A sources but the pupil states their own view. A short note: many pupils will have a personal story about walking or travelling to school; welcome these. Qur'an 25:63 describes the servants of the Most Merciful as those who walk on the earth with humility; a teacher may mention it as a reflection, not as part of the exam.

teach.heading: Compare forms
teach.note: Highlight that all three forms persuade but with different features. Ask pupils which is easiest to control and why. For EAL pupils: 'Dear Editor' and 'Yours faithfully' are conventions of formal letters.

teach.heading: Worked model: plan and opening

model.problem: Plan and open the article on 'Children should walk or cycle to school'.
steps: Headline: a punchy pun or question.
Opening: a short personal anecdote or striking image.
State your view clearly.
Plan three paragraphs: health, independence, community; one counter-argument; a call to action.
model.answer: HEADLINE: Time to Take the Long Way. Every morning on Elm Road, the traffic crawls and the pavements are empty. Yet the quickest journey is not always the best one. As someone who walks twenty minutes to school each day, I believe that every child who can should walk or cycle, because the journey makes us healthier, more independent and better neighbours.

teach.note: Read the plan and the opening paragraph. Ask pupils to annotate: headline, anecdote, direct address, claim, sign-posting. Point out that the opening is under 90 words and sets out the line of argument.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which opening best suits a persuasive school-magazine article?
options: Every morning on Elm Road, the traffic crawls and the pavements are empty. Yet the quickest journey is not always the best one.
Once upon a time there was a boy who went to school.
The school has 800 pupils and 12 buses.
check.why: A has a hook and a view. B is narrative; C informs without a stance.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is A. B is a story, C is a report.

teach.heading: Register and tone
bullets: Use 'I' sparingly and with purpose.
Avoid slang; use contractions rarely.
Address the reader: 'you', 'we', 'our school'.
Keep paragraphs short, linked by connectives.
teach.note: Say: friendly but formal. Idiom: 'to strike the right note'.

practice: Underline audience, purpose and form in a new task: a speech to parents about homework.
Write a headline with a pun for your article.
Write three topic sentences for your plan.
independent: Core: Write the headline and opening paragraph for the article.
Extend: Write the first two body paragraphs and a counter-argument.
Stretch: Write the complete 400-word article in 35 minutes.
exit: State the audience, purpose and form of the model task.
Why is a plan worth five minutes?
Big question: how do I make my view convincing and suited to the reader?
lessons.homework: Write a different opening (a speech version) for the same view, and list the changes from the article version.
lessons.send: SEND: give a planning frame (headline, hook, three reasons, counter-argument, call to action). EAL/international: pre-teach 'strapline', 'headline', 'counter-argument', 'campaign'; idiom 'a hook' (an opening that grabs attention); stems: 'I firmly believe that ...', 'Some people argue that ... however ...'. Cultural note: UK school magazines and local newspapers are common forums for pupil opinion. Stretch: shape the article for a hostile audience of parents who drive.

lessons.unit: P2-B-Q5: Paper 2 Section B: Question 5, viewpoint writing
lessons.title: Question 5: persuasive techniques, structure and polish
lessons.bigQuestion: Which techniques actually persuade, and when do they become too much?
objectives: Use rhetorical techniques accurately and with restraint
Structure a persuasive text with sign-posting and a counter-argument
Proofread for technical accuracy
successCriteria: All: use three persuasive devices correctly
Most: shape paragraphs with sign-posting and a counter-argument
Some: control register, vary sentence length and proofread to achieve a polished piece
lessons.crossCurricular: Speech and Debate; PSHE: healthy choices
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest persuasion, without exaggeration that misleads

keywords.def: an opposing view that you answer
words that guide the reader through the argument

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name three features of an article.
Write a rhetorical question about school uniforms.
Give a triplet about the benefits of exercise.

teach.heading: A FOREST of techniques

head: Letter
Technique
Example
rows: a mile takes about twenty minutes
walking is the best way to wake up
Why sit in traffic when you could stroll?
only one child in five walks

teach.note: Introduce the mnemonic A-F-O-R-E-S-T and say it is a memory aid, not a checklist: techniques must fit the argument. Warn about overuse: too many devices read as forced. Remind that statistics must be plausible and you may invent them, but keep them believable.

teach.heading: Structure with sign-posting
teach.note: Say that persuasion needs order. Move through the order and ask pupils to give a connective for each stage. Idiom: 'to have the last word'.

teach.heading: Worked model: a persuasive body paragraph

model.problem: Write a paragraph arguing that walking to school improves health, including a counter-argument.
steps: Topic sentence with a clear claim.
Evidence: a believable fact or statistic.
Technique: a rhetorical question and a triplet.
Counter-argument: 'Admittedly ...' followed by a reply.
Link back to the thesis.
model.answer: Walking to school makes children healthier. A mile on foot takes only twenty minutes, yet nearly half of pupils spend it slumped in the back seat of a car. Surely a little fresh air is a small price for brighter, steadier and calmer mornings? Admittedly, some families live too far away or are pressed for time; but even walking the last five minutes from a drop-off point can transform the day. A healthy journey is the first lesson of the day.

teach.note: Read the paragraph, then underline devices (question, triplet, emotive word, statistic, counter-argument). Ask pupils whether any device is overdone (no). Point out the register stays formal and the paragraph ends with a link back to the thesis.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which sentence uses a rhetorical question well?
options: A mile takes twenty minutes.
Amazing, awesome, fantastic walking!!!
Surely a little fresh air is a small price for a calmer morning?
check.why: C is a controlled rhetorical question that supports the argument. A is a fact; B is overdone and over-punctuated.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is C. A is a fact; B overuses devices without sense.

teach.heading: Proofreading for AO6
bullets: Check capitals, full stops and comma splices.
Check apostrophes (its / it's; children's).
Check spelling of tricky words (separate, definitely).
Read the final paragraph aloud in your head.
teach.note: Remind pupils that 16 marks are for technical accuracy. Teach a 'last five minutes' routine.

practice: Write one rhetorical question and one triplet for your own article.
Write a counter-argument sentence starting 'Admittedly'.
Proofread two sentences with three planted errors.
independent: Core: Write one body paragraph with three devices from A-F-O-R-E-S-T.
Extend: Write two body paragraphs with a counter-argument and a link back.
Stretch: Complete the 400-word article and annotate five techniques.
exit: Name three persuasive techniques.
Why must a counter-argument be answered?
Big question: when do techniques become too much?
lessons.homework: Write the final paragraph (a call to action) for the article and proofread it using the last-five-minutes routine.
lessons.send: SEND: give a technique card with example sentences; allow a phrase bank for sign-posting (firstly, however, finally). EAL/international: pre-teach 'rhetorical', 'triplet', 'emotive', 'admittedly'; idioms 'to have the last word', 'food for thought'; stems: 'Surely ...?', 'Admittedly ... but ...', 'It is time to ...'. Cultural note: UK persuasive writing uses understated humour and rhetorical questions; avoid insults. Stretch: construct a speech version with repetition and direct address.

lessons.unit: SL: Spoken Language endorsement (AO7 to AO9)
lessons.title: Spoken Language: planning a formal presentation
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I plan a talk that is clear, interesting and mine?
objectives: Choose a presentation topic and purpose that you can explain with authority
Plan a presentation of up to ten minutes with a clear structure
Prepare an opening and a closing that hold the audience's attention
successCriteria: All: choose a topic and three main points
Most: plan an introduction, a sequence of points and a conclusion with evidence
Some: shape the talk with a hook, signposting, varied techniques and anticipated questions
lessons.crossCurricular: All subjects: oral communication; Citizenship: public speaking
lessons.smsc: Moral and social: truthfulness (sidq), respect for the audience and courtesy in answering questions

keywords.def: formal grammar and vocabulary, not an accent
words that guide the audience through the talk

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name three features of a good opening in writing.
What are the three AOs for spoken language?
Name a topic you could talk about for five minutes with real knowledge.

teach.heading: What the endorsement is

head: AO
Skill
Evidence
rows: Presentation skills in a formal setting
Listen and respond to questions and feedback
grammar and vocabulary suited to formal speech

teach.note: Say: Spoken Language does not count towards the 9-1 grade; it is reported separately as Pass, Merit, Distinction or Not Classified, and is teacher-assessed. Pupils must meet all the criteria for a grade. Tell pupils that the presentation lasts up to about ten minutes and includes questions. AO7: present; AO8: listen and respond; AO9: use spoken Standard English. Teacher to check the school's current assessment criteria from AQA.

teach.heading: Plan the talk

timeline.label: 1. Hook
timeline.text: a question, anecdote or fact (30 seconds)

timeline.label: 2. Aim
timeline.text: state what you will explain and why it matters

timeline.label: 3. Points
timeline.text: three main points, each with an example

timeline.label: 4. Summary
timeline.text: return to the hook and recap

teach.note: Show the shape as a timeline. Ask pupils to decide where the audience will most easily lose attention and what they will do. Say that notes should be cue cards with keywords, not full sentences.

teach.heading: Worked model: an opening

model.problem: Write the opening of a five-minute presentation on 'Why every community needs a library'.
steps: Start with a hook: a question or striking fact.
State your aim and your three points.
Use signposting: 'First ... second ... finally'.
Use formal but natural Standard English.
model.answer: Good morning, everyone. How many of you have ever found an answer in a library that the internet could not give you? Today I want to persuade you that every community needs a library, and I will do so in three steps: first, how libraries help learning; second, how they bring people together; and finally, why they matter most to those who have the least.

teach.note: Read the opening aloud with a clear voice. Underline the hook (question), the aim and the signposting. Note the Standard English forms such as 'I will explain' and the polite end. Cultural note: UK audiences expect a direct start and not a long preamble.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is the best use of notes in a presentation?
options: Write the whole speech and read it word for word.
Use cue cards with keywords and signposts.
Use no notes at all and improvise.
check.why: B keeps eye contact and structure. A reads flatly; C risks losing the thread.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is B. A is too wordy and C has no aim.

teach.heading: Choosing a topic
bullets: Choose something you can explain and defend.
Make sure the audience can learn something.
Prepare three facts or examples.
Predict two questions and prepare answers.
teach.note: Pupils choose something they know and care about, with a teacher's agreement. Remind them the topic must allow questions. Idiom: 'to know your stuff'.

practice: Write your hook, aim and three points on a single cue card.
Write two questions you expect from the audience.
Draft the final sentence of your presentation.
independent: Core: Write a five-line plan of your presentation using the five stages.
Extend: Write the full opening (80 words) in Standard English.
Stretch: Write the opening and closing and plan a visual or example that supports your main point.
exit: Name the three AOs for spoken language.
Why use cue cards rather than reading a script?
Big question: how do I plan a talk that is mine?
lessons.homework: Prepare a two-minute version of your opening and main points; record yourself and write three improvements.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a presentation plan template with sentence starters and allow a short practice with a trusted adult; consider the teacher's reasonable adjustments for speech and anxiety. EAL/international: pre-teach 'presentation', 'hook', 'signposting', 'cue card'; idiom 'to break the ice' = to ease nerves at the start; stems: 'Today I will explain ...', 'First ..., second ..., finally ...', 'Thank you for listening'. Cultural note: UK presentation style is direct and polite; an accent is fine, Standard English is about grammar. Stretch: plan a rhetorical device that frames the talk.

lessons.unit: SL: Spoken Language endorsement (AO7 to AO9)
lessons.title: Spoken Language: delivery, Standard English and answering questions
lessons.bigQuestion: How can my voice and my answers show confidence and respect?
objectives: Use voice, pace and eye contact to present with confidence
Use spoken Standard English accurately
Respond to questions and feedback clearly and courteously
successCriteria: All: speak clearly and audibly in Standard English
Most: vary pace and tone and answer questions with evidence
Some: respond to difficult questions diplomatically and build on feedback
lessons.crossCurricular: Drama: voice and presence; Citizenship: debate
lessons.smsc: Moral and social: courtesy (adab) in listening and answering
starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name the three parts of a presentation plan.
Say one sentence in Standard English about your topic.
Explain the difference between accent and Standard English.

teach.heading: Standard English in speech

misconception.wrong: 'I have to change my accent to speak Standard English.'
misconception.right: 'Standard English is grammar and vocabulary; I can keep my accent and say "we were" and "I did not".'

teach.note: State clearly that accent is not the issue: Standard English concerns grammar and vocabulary, and every accent is welcome. Ask pupils to correct sentences orally. Cultural note: in casual British talk many people say 'we was' or 'I ain't', but in a formal presentation we use Standard forms.

teach.heading: Delivery checklist
teach.note: Practise the checklist as a class with a one-sentence line. Ask each pupil to model one, for example pace. Remind pupils to breathe and pause after key points.

teach.heading: Worked model: answering a question

model.problem: An audience member asks: 'Libraries are old-fashioned; why not just use the internet?' Give a model answer.
steps: Thank the questioner.
Restate the question to show you listened.
Answer with a reason and an example.
Acknowledge a fair point; check they are satisfied.
model.answer: Thank you, that is a fair question. You are asking whether the internet makes libraries unnecessary. I would say not, because many people do not have a quiet place or reliable access at home, and a librarian can help you find reliable sources. The internet is useful, and I use it too, but a library offers something different. Does that answer your question?

teach.note: Read the question and answer. Show the steps: thank, clarify, answer with evidence, check. Note the model includes a polite correction and an honest 'I do not know' response, which is acceptable and shows truthfulness.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which response to a challenging question is best?
options: 'That is a silly question.'
'Thank you; that is a fair point. I would answer that ...'
'I will not talk about that.'
check.why: B is courteous and engages with the question. A is rude; C avoids the question.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is B. A dismisses the questioner; C avoids the question.

teach.heading: Feedback and AO8
bullets: Listen to the whole question first.
Pause, then answer.
Accept feedback politely; use it.
Ask for clarification when needed.
teach.note: Say that listening matters as much as speaking: AO8 asks you to respond to questions and feedback. Idiom: 'to take on board' = to accept and use feedback.

practice: Say your opening sentence in Standard English with clear pace.
Answer a partner's question using the four-step model.
Correct five spoken non-standard sentences orally.
independent: Core: Present your two-minute opening to a partner and answer two questions.
Extend: Present for four minutes with a hook and signposting; note your partner's feedback.
Stretch: Present for five minutes, answer three questions and write a short reflection on feedback.
exit: Is Standard English an accent? Explain.
Name two features of confident delivery.
Big question: how can voice and answers show confidence and respect?
lessons.homework: Practise your full presentation twice and write one improvement target for each of voice, pace and language.
lessons.send: SEND: allow additional preparation time, cue cards in large print and a small audience; reasonable adjustments to be agreed with the SENCo. EAL/international: pre-teach 'audible', 'intelligible', 'clarify', 'diplomatic'; idiom 'to take on board'; stems: 'Thank you for your question', 'What I mean is ...', 'Does that answer your question?'. Cultural note: in British settings it is polite to thank a questioner and to disagree gently. Stretch: field a hostile question without raising your voice.
